newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romanians vote in cliff-hanger presidential fight.
newsitem.headline: Romanians vote in cliff-hanger presidential fight.

text.p: Romanians vote on Sunday in a presidential contest that could end the grip ex-communists have held on the Balkan country since its bloody 1989 revolution.

The academic anti-communist Emil Constantinescu is locked in a tight run-off battle against Ion Iliescu, who has ruled for the nearly seven years since Stalinist dictator Nicolae Ceausescu was ousted and executed.
Unlike Iliescu, tainted by holding high office under Ceausescu and accused of ruling in an arrogant and demagogic manner, Constantinescu held no position under communism.

He pledges a new era of clean government, better economic management and reforms to stop living standards in impoverished Romania lagging further behind ex-communist near neighbours like Hungary and Poland.
The mild-mannered geology professor charges Iliescu led a corrupt, incompetent administration that failed to remedy Romania's fiscal woes and crumbling infrastructure.

He has taken heart from the first round of voting two weeks ago when Romanians, fed up with eking out a living on salaries of some $100 a month, ousted Iliescu's leftist party from government and installed Constantinescu's reform group.
In bitter television debates, Iliescu has played on the conservatism and fears of many Romanians and said a victory for him would protect people from the costs of social change.

"I am convinced voters will understand that to preserve national unity and peace for coming generations they must vote for Iliescu," said Adrian Nastase, leader of Iliescu's Party of Social Democracy.
There have been no reliable opinion polls since the first round and the contest is thought too close to call.
Town dwellers and the young are expected to back the challenger's vision of reform while pensioners and rural voters may plump for Iliescu's message of caution.
"I have confidence in Constantinescu. I don't expect to live like a German or American but I hope for a better life in a few years," said Stefan Gruia, 47, an engineer.
"I will vote for Iliescu. If Constantinescu wins prices will go up and life will be unbearable for us pensioners," said Gabriel Visarion, a retired office worker from Bucharest.

Some 15,000 polling stations open at 6 a.m. (0400 gmt) and exit polls will give the first indication of the result shortly after the last vote is cast at midnight (2200 gmt). Official results will trickle in throughout Monday.
A high turnout may favour Iliescu, who will also benefit if his support holds up in the country's many backward villages.
But Constantinescu may benefit from disillusion with the negative campaigning style of the 66-year-old president, who has reportedly been worn out by the election struggle.
With a mandatory 48-hour pre-voting campaign break keeping the candidates off televisions on Saturday, news programmes resorted to advising voters how to avoid spoiling ballots.
Poor printing of the ballot papers means ink can easily transfer from one page to another, rendering the vote invalid.
Private PRO TV news used a jingle to urge their viewers to "blow and shake," the paper until it is dry enough to be dropped into the ballot box.
